newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian consumers emerge with tentative new spending.
newsitem.headline: Canadian consumers emerge with tentative new spending.

text.p: After a lengthy spending drought, tight-fisted Canadian consumers appear to be opening their wallets again, but some economic indicators suggest the consumer recovery may be tenuous.

A survey by the Conference Board of Canada released on Thursday put consumer confidence at its highest point in seven years, after a brutal recession in the early 1990s, followed by a sluggish recovery.

"I think this is a recovery that you want to keep observing," said Peter Drake, deputy chief economist at Toront-Dominion Bank. "You don't want to take it for granted. You keep looking at the numbers because you remember where we've come from."
Consumer spending rose 1.3 percent in the first quarter of this year, slightly higher than in the last quarter of 1996.

But other indicators give mixed signals. New car sales, for example, rose 1.8 percent in May after falling 4.9 percent in April. Retail sales were up 1.1 percent in April following a 0.8 percent decline in March.
Meanwhile, building permits -- an early indicator of future demand for labor and construction material -- fell 12 percent in May after rising 9.3 percent in April.
However, the overall trend this year has been positive for consumer confidence, economists said.
"I think the recovery is solid," Drake said, although he added: "People could get nervous again relatively quickly."
Canadian consumers in the 1990s have been faced with high unemployment, job instability, high taxes, new free trade agreements, deep government cutbacks and corporate restructurings.
"There's probably some lingering nervousness," Drake said. "It wouldn't take a large sign (of weakness) to make people say 'Whoa'."
The Conference Board of Canada, an economic research institute, said that 59.4 percent of consumers polled at the beginning of June felt this summer was a good time to buy "big ticket" items.
The board linked the confidence to optimism about the job market and low interest rates.
But a key question is whether Canadians have the money to pay for shopping sprees, said economist Mike McCracken, chairman of Ottawa-based Informetrica.
"Unless real disposable income gains come along, there could be a real problem in the future," he said on Thursday in a telephone interview.

Disposable income rose by about one percent -- less than the annual rate of inflation -- in 1996 and was unchanged in the first quarter of 1997. Economists project personal income will likely keep pace with inflation this year or grow slightly.
Year-over-year inflation was 1.8 percent for Canada in June, statistics released on Thursday showed.
Healthy job creation is the other key to spurring consumer confidence, McCracken added.
The job market has picked up, with 52,000 jobs created in June and the unemployment rate dropping to 9.1 percent from 9.5 percent in May.
"We've begun to get some sense of forward movement," McCracken said.

Youth unemployment, remains high, however, rising 0.3 percentage points in June to 17.5 percent. Public sector downsizing, which has battered the job market in recent years, was also continuing, he said.
